p: Ben Sira warns that money corrupts, as the Law and Paul do.
b: The Law forbids bribes "because a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deuteronomy 16:19; compare Exodus 23:8). Paul warns that those who want to get rich fall into a trap, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:9-10). Ben Sira's point is practical as well as moral: a poor man cannot win a fight with a rich one, because money buys judges and even kings. The Hebrew in Kahana says gold "has made many reckless" and "leads astray the heart of nobles."
orig: πολλοὺς γὰρ ἀπώλεσεν τὸ χρυσίον (pollous gar apōlesen to chrysion), "for gold has destroyed many"

a: do not pile wood on his fire
p: Proverbs uses the same picture for a quarrel kept alive by talk.
b: Proverbs says, "When the wood runs out, the fire dies, / and when there is no gossip, the fighting calms down" (Proverbs 26:20), and the next verse compares a quarrelsome man to charcoal on embers (Proverbs 26:21). The "man who talks too much" (Greek glōssōdēs, "all tongue") is the person whose quarrel grows with every word you answer. James calls the tongue a fire (James 3:5-6).

a: every one of us is liable to be punished
p: Ben Sira grounds mercy toward the repentant in the guilt everyone shares.
b: The Greek en epitimiois means "under penalties," liable to punishment; the Hebrew in Kahana says זְכֹר כִּי כֻּלָּנוּ חַיָּבִים, "remember that all of us are guilty." This matches the 66 books: "For there is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20), and Paul, "For all sinned, and all lack the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Paul draws the same practical lesson as Ben Sira: restore a fallen brother gently, "Look to yourself, in case you are tempted as well" (Galatians 6:1). Jesus' story of the lost son condemns the brother who will not welcome a sinner home (Luke 15:25-32).
orig: πάντες ἐσμὲν ἐν ἐπιτίμοις (pantes esmen en epitimois)

a: Do not slight a man when he is old
p: The Law commands respect for the aged, and Ben Sira gives the reason: we are all heading there.
b: Leviticus says, "Rise up before gray hair, and honor the face of the old" (Leviticus 19:32). Ben Sira adds a reason that anyone can feel: "there are those among us who are aging too." The Hebrew in Kahana says it more personally: "remember that you will be counted among the old."

a: Do not gloat over anyone who has died
p: Proverbs forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls; Ben Sira extends it to death itself.
b: Proverbs says, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad, / and when he trips, keep your heart from cheering" (Proverbs 24:17). Ben Sira's reason is the fate everyone shares: "we all come to our end." The Hebrew in Kahana says זְכֹר כֻּלָּנוּ נֶאֱסָפִים, "remember: all of us are gathered in," the old phrase for dying and joining one's ancestors (Genesis 25:8). The KJV's "thy greatest enemy" comes from a longer Greek text; see the variant.

p: The Greek "proverbs" stands for a Hebrew word that also means riddles.
b: The Greek paroimiai, "proverbs, sayings," is the word the Greek Proverbs uses for its own title. The Hebrew in Kahana has וּבְחִידֹתֵיהֶם הִתְרַפֵּשׂ, "and busy yourself with their riddles" (chidot), the word of Proverbs 1:6, "the words of the wise and their riddles." A scribe learned by memorizing and puzzling over the sayings of earlier teachers, as Ben Sira says in 39:1-3.
orig: ἐν ταῖς παροιμίαις αὐτῶν ἀναστρέφου (en tais paroimiais autōn anastrephou)

p: Ben Sira's students were trained to serve rulers, so this is career advice.
b: The Greek leitourgēsai megistasin means "to serve great men," to be of use in the courts of the powerful. In Ben Sira's day Judea was ruled by Greek kings, first the Ptolemies of Egypt and then, from about 200 BC, the Seleucids of Syria, with a high priest and a council of elders in Jerusalem. Educated scribes served as advisers, envoys and record-keepers. In 39:4 Ben Sira says the scribe will serve among great men and appear before rulers.

a: for they in turn were taught by their fathers
p: Wisdom passes from father to son, from teacher to student.
b: Moses says, "Ask your father, and he will tell you, / your old ones, and they will explain" (Deuteronomy 32:7), and Bildad tells Job to learn from the former generation (Job 8:8-10). Ben Sira's chain of learning, the old learning from their fathers and teaching the young, is the same idea that later Jewish tradition put at the head of the Mishnah's tractate Avot: the Torah handed down from Moses through a line of teachers. Ben Sira himself is a link in such a chain.

a: give ground to an insolent man
p: The Greek is unclear: do not leave your place, or do not rise up in anger?
b: The Greek exanastēs apo prosōpou means "rise up from before the face of." It may mean "do not get up and leave" (give way to him), or "do not rise up against him." The KJV reads "Rise not up in anger." The Hebrew in Kahana, אַל תָּזוּחַ מִפְּנֵי לֵץ, means "do not budge before a scoffer," and supports the first reading: if you give ground, he will sit in your place and wait to catch you out in your words. The Plain follows that sense.
orig: μὴ ἐξαναστῇς ἀπὸ προσώπου ὑβριστοῦ (mē exanastēs apo prosōpou hybristou)

a: Do not stand good for more than you can manage
p: Ben Sira takes up Proverbs' warnings about guaranteeing loans, but is more willing to allow it.
b: To "stand good for" a person is to guarantee his debt (Greek engyaō; Hebrew 'arav). Proverbs warns hard against it: "My son, if you have stood good for your neighbor, / if you have struck palms for an outsider," get yourself free at once (Proverbs 6:1-5; compare Proverbs 11:15; Proverbs 22:26-27). Ben Sira softens the rule: do it only within your means, and expect to pay. In 29:14-20 he praises the good man who stands good for his neighbor and warns of the ruin it can bring.
orig: μὴ ἐγγυήσῃ ὑπὲρ δύναμίν σου (mē engyēsē hyper dynamin sou)

a: Do not take a judge to court
p: A judge's colleagues will side with him because of his rank.
b: The Greek says "they will judge for him according to his glory (rank, reputation)." In a world without independent courts, a lawsuit against a judge would be heard by his friends. The Hebrew in Kahana reads "for he will judge as he pleases." The Law demands that judges not show favor (Deuteronomy 16:18-20), but Ben Sira describes how things often were.
orig: κατὰ γὰρ τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ κρινοῦσιν αὐτῷ (kata gar tēn doxan autou krinousin autō)

a: Do not pick a fight with a hot-tempered man
p: Proverbs gives the same warning about hot-tempered company.
b: Proverbs says, "Do not keep company with a man ruled by anger, / and do not go along with someone full of rage" (Proverbs 22:24), for you may learn his ways. Ben Sira adds the danger of the open road: in the desert, where there is no one to help, a man who thinks nothing of blood may kill you. Travel through the Judean wilderness was dangerous, as the story of the man who fell among robbers on the road to Jericho shows (Luke 10:30).

a: he will not be able to keep a word quiet
t: A fool cannot keep a secret
p: Proverbs contrasts the gossip with the faithful friend who keeps a matter covered.
b: The Greek logon stexai means "to keep a word covered," to keep a confidence. Proverbs says, "One who goes around telling tales lays bare what was said in confidence, / but one with a faithful spirit keeps the matter under cover" (Proverbs 11:13). The Hebrew in Kahana uses poteh, the naive or simple person of Proverbs: כִּי לֹא יוּכַל לְכַסּוֹת סוֹדֶךָ, "for he cannot cover your secret."

a: you cannot know what it will give birth to
p: Ben Sira borrows Proverbs' picture of time "giving birth" to the unknown.
b: Proverbs says, "Don't brag about tomorrow, / since you cannot know what a day will give birth to" (Proverbs 27:1). Ben Sira uses the same verb (Greek tiktō, "give birth"; Hebrew in Kahana yeled) for a secret told before a stranger: you cannot know what it will lead to. The Talmud quotes a Ben Sira saying with the same phrase, "you do not know what a day will bring" (Yevamot 63b).

a: do not let anyone walk off with your good fortune
p: The Greek is hard; the Hebrew says do not drive good fortune away from yourself.
b: The Greek mē anapheretō soi charin literally means "and let him not carry off (or bring back) favor for you." It is unclear whether the danger is that a person you confide in will take your good standing away, or will "repay" your trust badly, as the KJV takes it ("requite thee with a shrewd turn"). The Hebrew in Kahana reads וְאַל תַּדִּיחַ מֵעָלֶיךָ הַטּוֹבָה, "and do not drive good fortune away from yourself." The Plain follows the sense the Hebrew supports.
orig: καὶ μὴ ἀναφερέτω σοι χάριν (kai mē anapheretō soi charin)
